I am a big fan of a "single source of truth" with minimal likelyhood of getting out of sync.   That being said, the source code repo is the ultimate source of truth, and having the developer maintain basic essential documentation is needed to keep them in sync.    The user/admin docs can more easily reference a single MD file in the source repo than to generally say "see the follow source file directories and parse them yourself".
also, while in the same repo, it is eminently possible to have an automated test compare the source code with the documentation to flag any inconsistencies.

> 1. When the inherited environment has APPTAINER variable of same name suffix as a set SINGULARITY environment variable, the APPTAINER value shall have precedence.

I concur with @truatpasteurdotfr, that should emit a warning.

> 2. When a SINGULARITY environment variable is set, and the APPTAINER environment with the same suffix is not set, copy the value of the SINGULARITY environment variable to a newly created APPTAINER variable with same name suffix.

I concur with @truatpasteurdotfr again, but this should also be a warning of depreciation. 

> 3. When creating the environment for a child process, enumerate all APPTAINER variable values from (1, 2) above, and create a new set of SINGULARITY environment variables with the same value and name suffix as the APPTAINER variable.

Yes. This is a good idea to ensure compatibility for all cases.

> I think that supporting any APPTAINER* variable should not be in Apptainer 1.0.0, and we can consider it for Apptainer 1.1.0.

These are not major or high risk changes, I would strongly push for them to be in 1.0.0 so the entire 1.x series won't have any major breaking changes after the first release.

Hi @vsoch, removing this code is not intended as a slight at all toward your work, which is absolutely fantastic. Let me ask it this way...

Did you you follow an open public specification/interface that is community maintained and standardized or did you reverse engineer the API? If it is the latter, therein lies the problem.

While the API itself is not commercial, it is absolutely commercially controlled. Considering we are a non-commercially affiliated community, it doesn't make sense for us to support commercially controlled APIs when there are open, standard, and actively maintained APIs already available for doing exactly this which are also more in-alignment with the rest of the container community (e.g. OCI/ORAS).

There just weren't that many developers that were using it, and I suspect if there were, there would have been more docs written.

> While the API itself is not commercial, it is absolutely commercially controlled. 

GitHub packages is also commercially controlled - are you going to remove oras for that? This is a fairly weak argument because many OSS tools and projects are developed first by commercial entities (and we use them). 

> Considering we are a non-commercially affiliated community, it doesn't make sense for us to support commercially controlled APIs when there are open, standard, and actively maintained APIs already available for doing exactly this which are also more in-alignment with the rest of the container community (e.g. OCI/ORAS).

The entirely of OCI is also made up of commercial vendors - should we nix that one too? Also, Singularity Registry server (and any other tool that uses the library API) is not commercial. I suppose you don't mind stepping on those as well?

I do not think using `~/.singularity` if `~/.apptainer` doesn't exist will lead to a good user experience. In general I don't think we should be transparently writing to `~/.singularity`, so with that assumption we should only use it for reading.

There will be operations that require a user configuration directory to be available for writing, such as the `instance` command group which tracks state of spawned containers. This means we will need to automatically create a `~/.apptainer` directory.

With the proposed behavior, the use of a command group like `instance` will cause configuration that appeared to exist for the user to suddenly disappear because an `~/.apptainer` directory has been created. We should start with the assumption that an `~/.apptainer` directory exists, regardless of the existence of a `~/.singularity` directory.

We have two types of data within user home directories to consider and handle separately:
1. User configuration data (remotes, oci credentials, pgp keys)
2. User image cache data (cached SIF images, oci blobs)
3. Container state data (meta data of tracked container processes)


1. User configuration data
I think the best user experience will be to offer migration commands to update user configurations in a new, potentially empty `~/.apptainer` directory from a `~/.singularity` directory if it exists.

The two major types of user configuration could be migrated with the following commands:
```
apptainer legacy migrate gpgkeys
apptainer legacy migrate remotes 
```

2. User image cache data
It would be ideal to merge image cache data in `~/.apptainer` and `~/.singularity` into a single cache without data duplication.
Unfortunately, the way the image cache packages in use by Apptainer are not designed to allow merging of multiple image or blob caches for use during an operation. This would take significant effort to update internal and external packages to make a reality.

Instead I propose that Apptainer automatically uses `~/.apptainer` for image/blob caching and we communicate to users that they can use the an existing cache created from a Singularity installation by simply setting `APPTAINER_CACHEDIR=~/.singularity`.

3. Container state data
This should always be under `~/.apptainer` for containers spawned by Apptainer. It does not make sense to me to try to guarantee that instances, and their resulting state, created by an Apptainer installation can be managed by a Singularity installation. And vice versa.


Based off of these thoughts, I will create a pr for commands to migrate user configuration data

@preney If the decision is made to allow unprivileged users to build a definition file, how are we going implement it?

Would it be the default or be opted-in with a flag? If we use a flag, how should singularity behave when root privileges are detected? How do we ensure reproducibility?

I feel that the default should be to allow users to build with a definition file. 

Syntax could be added to the definition file to assert it requires root privileges and so running such without those perms may or may not work properly or be reproducible. It is also possible to have the "opposite" syntax, i.e., syntax that asserts the definition file can be run without root permissions. Given there are existing definition files the latter might be preferred. (Either way should work.)

That said, it might not be unreasonable to have "version" syntax in the definition file to allow dealing with past semantics, permitting things to evolve forwards, e.g., if breaking some backwards compatibility. The lack of version syntax would imply the original rules and the version syntax would imply whatever that version requires.

I am thinking a version syntax idea is probably a good one since the existing definition file syntax IMHO isn't really all that reproducible or "secure": it heavily depends on the existing shell and the commands that are available on the system being used and IMHO should really evolve to be shell and command independent and/or formally assert required shell/commands that can be check prior to running the definition file. Getting to such a point would likely take place over a number of "syntax versions" as that would not happen overnight.

Hi @ShamrockLee , unfortunately it won't be as simple as removing `Geteuid() != 0`, the issue there is that the container image build is occurring in the same context as `apptainer exec` since it call it behind the scene, so as an unprivileged user you are not authorized to specify an alternate configuration to fully control what's being mounted inside the container during a build (and build is relying on this to override the config specified by an administrator in the build context), explaining why you removed the configuration check here https://github.com/apptainer/apptainer/pull/250/files#diff-15947087c721a58de48322e21fffa6a6d81e73df717c4749a39522198e27b56eL445 to force build to run correctly, but the side effect of this:
- `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/group` are mounted in the container during build
- your home directory is mounted in the container during build
- the build is subject to admin config restrictions like `user bind control = no`, `allow container dir = no`, `limit container paths`
So build may randomly failed based on the configuration set.

So far home mount could be easily fixed by using `--no-home` flag or `--no-mount=home`, `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/group` are requiring more changes to disable mount as unprivileged user, thinking about using `--no-mount` flag for that.
But for config restrictions that could be potentially set, this is an obvious blocker for security reasons, so it could be only handled through checks and aborting gracefully by informing users that it won't be possible to run build command due to restrictions set by the configuration file.

@marian-babik @DrDaveD This is a flaw in glibc, `grantpt` call `chown` if `uid != user_uid` and/or `gid != 5 (tty)`, when using user namespace the kernel after opening `/dev/ptmx` creates the pseudoterminal `/dev/pts/X` with `uid = user_uid` and `gid = user_gid`, so glibc in `grantpt` try to force gid to be 5 on `/dev/pts/X`, but `granpt` checks on uid and gid are rather weak in glibc, it should call `access` before calling `chown` which is requiring privileges for this case, and even if tty group was mapped correctly in the user namespace (note: this is impossible to do from apptainer without setuid), `chown` would return an `EPERM` error in any case.

Note that the example you gave is working fine with centos:8 / rockylinux:8, confirming this is a glibc issue.

To be clear, there is nothing that can be done at apptainer level to fix that, and if you really want/need to make it works with centos:7 images, you would have to create a LD_PRELOAD fix by first creating a shared lib with `grantpt` as a no-op call:
```
cat > inject.c <<EOF
int grantpt(int fd) { return 0; }
EOF
```
Compile it:
```
gcc -shared -fPIC -o inject.so inject.c
```

Inject it inside container:
```
export SINGULARITY_BIND=inject.so:/mnt/inject.so
export LD_PRELOAD=/mnt/inject.so
singularity exec -u docker://centos:7 python -c "import pty;pty.spawn(['echo', 'jupyter'])"
```

I see.  Even on a CentOS 7 host, the following command works:
```
$ singularity  exec  docker://rockylinux:8 /usr/libexec/platform-python -c "import pty;pty.spawn(['echo', 'jupyter'])"
INFO:    Using cached SIF image
jupyter
```
because the glibc in the container can handle the unprivileged user namespace.

@cyyzero Fuse file descriptors are all opened in stage 1, stage 1 is a forked step executing Go code in host user namespace, but opened `/dev/fuse` descriptors in the host user namespace couldn't be used inside a container user namespace for security reasons, that's why when a container is using a new container user namespace, we need to reopen them inside this new user namespace to make them usable and we also need to re-associate them to their previous file descriptor ID with dup3 call, re-association is important because the file descriptor ID is shared by at least two separate processes which require to operate on the same file descriptor ID

I see, you are right.  The problem was introduced in apptainer 1.0.0 via apptainer/singularity#6224 which was imported from a Sylabs PR.  There the ldconfig path was put into the configuration file at compile time rather than searching $PATH at run time.  The problem must also exist in singularity-ce >= 3.9.0 and greater.

The good news is that this is already fixed in the main branch via #367 and so will be in 1.1.0.  It goes back to searching $PATH by default and includes the user's $PATH when running unprivileged.  I verified it by installing a package built from the current main branch in my image and changing the configuration to set `allow setuid = no` with this line:
```
sed -i 's/^allow setuid = yes/allow setuid = no/' /etc/apptainer/apptainer.conf
```
Still, it would be nicer of course if the workaround was not needed.

Another way to make it work even with apptainer 1.0.x should be the following:
```
export APPTAINER_BINDPATH=/.singularity.d/libs
```
That doesn't get rid of the `Could not find any nv libraries on this host!` warning but it does put the libraries into $LD_LIBRARY_PATH where they should be visible to nvidia-smi.  It shouldn't be hard to make a PR that also looks for the libraries in /.singularity.d/libs (or $LD_LIBRARY_PATH to be more general) and uses them instead of the original paths.

Keep in mind that a SIF file is not directly mounted, it is a set of partitions.  I believe that if the squashfs partition is marked overlay it might work.  You can probably do that with an `apptainer sif` command.

An overlay also has to be in the format expected by overlayfs, that is, with an "upper" and "work" directory.  Additional files go in the "upper" directory.  The "work" directory I believe is mostly for keeping track of removals and it is in a format that's best left only to be created by overlayfs.  I suggest creating an ext3 overlay first as described in the [documentation](https://apptainer.org/docs/user/main/persistent_overlays.html), then run apptainer as root with --overlay to create the additions you want, then you can directly mount the ext3 to see what its contents are.
I don't see an option to modify the flags, so you'd probably need to dump the partition (to a file, redirect stdout), then delete the partition, and add it back with the overlay parttype.

I think the problem is something peculiar to that image.  I don't think that normally the current directory is searched for libraries.

## whitelist

Two of the signatures are whitelisted.

```
# /etc/apptainer/ecl.toml

activated = true
[[execgroup]]
mode = "whitelist"
dirpath = "/home/janderson"
keyfp = ["338D307ED3F6E64B625B58F73E2CBBC2C983B7AB","36303D4322865BC6BDADA3E3E795716FAC8D8ED0"]
```

No keys imported, so failure.

```
$ apptainer exec alpine.sif sh -c 'echo "Hello, world!"'
FATAL:   while checking container image with ECL: image not signed by required entities
```

Importing just one of the whitelisted keys, so success.

```
$ sudo apptainer key import --global test2
Key with fingerprint 36303D4322865BC6BDADA3E3E795716FAC8D8ED0 successfully added to the public keyring

$ apptainer exec alpine.sif sh -c 'echo "Hello, world!"'
Hello, world!
```

Going back to your original issue with the `--nv` flag, I am able to replicate on a Fedora 36 laptop with an NVIDIA GPU.  And I'm also able to fix the issue.  

#### The short answer
Make a backup copy and edit `$APPTAINER_HOME/etc/apptainer/nvliblist.conf` (where `$APPTAINER_HOME` refers to the base of your installation. In your case the file may just be located in `/etc` since you installed from rpm.)

Remove the following:
```
libGLdispatch.so
libglx.so
libGLX.so
```
Try again and your original container should run glxgears.  If you have a laptop like mine you may have to set the following before running the container to force the laptop to use the discrete (NVIDIA) graphics card instead of integrated graphics.
```
export __NV_PRIME_RENDER_OFFLOAD_PROVIDER=NVIDIA-G0 __GLX_VENDOR_LIBRARY_NAME=nvidia
```
#### The long answer

The `--nv` and `--nvccli` options work differently.  The `--nvccli` option can obtain system-specific information about the GPU driver and user-side libraries that are installed as well as where to find them.  The `--nv` option on the other hand is pretty dumb.  It has a list of all the user-libraries that might be important to run GPU enabled containers (`nvliblist.conf`).  It looks through all libraries installed on the host system and whatever matches it bind mounts into the container.  

This dumb strategy usually works, in part because the user facing libraries that allow programs to interact with the NVIDIA kernel module are most often compiled to allow compatibility with older glibc versions.

Now, there has be some disagreement in the past about which libraries actually belong in `nvliblist.conf`.  And I think this issue shows why.  It sounds like we now have a situation where a few libraries on the Fedora 36 host are compiled using the latest greatest glibc and can't link to the glibc in the container.  But luckily, these libraries are already installed in the container as well (at `/usr/lib64`).  Furthermore, the libraries in the container are properly compiled against the glibc in the container.  

So the solution is to delete the offending libraries from `nvliblist.conf`.  This will work as long as the containers you try to run on this host have `libGLdispatch.so*`, and `lib<glx,GLX>.so*` installed in them if they rely on them.

The other way is to always avoid using kernel overlayfs if the lower layer is fuse.  There is in fact already code checking to see if the lower layer is fuse, and when using only overlayfs it errors out early. @DrDaveD The CAP_SYS_ADMIN privilege is required to create a checkpoint for a running process on a singularity container using CRIU and to be able to restart it in the future. This is not possible for the actual service because we must grant administrator privileges to that user. CAP_CHECKPOINT_RESTORE, the capability we requested, supports Checkpoint/Restore without administrator privileges. This is applied to the latest kernel(5.9), but backported for RHEL8 or derived os. Therefore, the CAP is also available in CentOS8. As I know, the Singularity Code does not have that part of the content, but I'm not sure if it's just a help message or if it affects the application of the feature. If there is no problem with the actual application, I will close the issue.

Thanks for posting the issue, it's not something I had thought to test, and it is unfortunate because I don't know a good solution for it.

The [ssh source code](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/master/readconf.c#L2255) is checking for either uid 0 or the current user id.  With unprivileged user namespaces (and without fakeroot), it's not an option for it to show up as uid 0, because the only mapped user id is the current user id; everybody else is mapped to `nobody`.

One way around it is to run with `--fakeroot` as you saw; that makes the files appear to be owned as uid 0.  The reason why it is not working without fakeroot is that the `squashfuse_ll` program does not support the `-o uid=NN` option, so apptainer cannot tell it to show all files as owned by you.  Apptainer will pass that option if the program is `squashfuse`, because that supports it.  I just verified it by temporary renaming the `squashfuse_ll` programs.  The `squashfuse_ll` program has so much better performance than `squashfuse`, however, that it's really not worth considering making it the default because of this issue.

I looked briefly at possibly making a patch to `squashfuse_ll` to add this option, but at first glance it looked like the low-level FUSE API that `squashfuse_ll` uses may make it so that is not even possible.  The `-o uid=NN` option in `squashfuse` is in fact implemented by the FUSE library, not `squashfuse` itself.

The only other idea I have for a workaround at this point is that the problem does not happen with sandboxes, which you can get for example temporarily with the `--unsquash` option.   I suppose it would also be possible to make an action command option to have it prefer `squashfuse` over `squashfuse_ll`, although that would be a bit of a challenge to implement because of the internal image driver api that is being used for that.

> I looked briefly at possibly making a patch to squashfuse_ll to add this option, but at first glance it looked like the low-level FUSE API that squashfuse_ll uses may make it so that is not even possible. 

No I think I was remembering wrong.  I do see the implementation of the `stat` function there returning a `uid` and `gid`, so  `-o uid` and `-o gid` options probably could be implemented.  Then the next question would be how Apptainer could figure out whether or not to pass them depending on the version of `squashfuse_ll`.

I made a [squashfuse pull request](https://github.com/vasi/squashfuse/pull/77) to add these options to the low level interface.  Apptainer could parse the help message looking for the option when deciding whether or not to invoke it with `squashfuse_ll`, and it could include that patch with the `squashfuse_ll` that it builds in rpm & debian packaging.

It seems to be a packaging issue. The (built) package requires a set of dependencies, each with a minimum version. It seems to be a common thing, where one package says, e.g. (completely made up) httpd requires OpenSSL >= 1.1.5 so if the system has only OpenSSL 1.0.x the package would not install.

This is already done with many packages. I can't upgrade, say, httpd because I do not have the appropriate version of OpenSSL that is required. I am proposing that the Apptainer RPM also specify minimum versions of its dependencies. At least, specify the versions used to build the RPM. In that way, when one upgrades apptainer, `dnf/yum` will not apply the upgrade because the system lacks appropriate versions of the dependencies.

Currently, the upgrade succeeds giving no indication that a "broken" version of apptainer has been installed, "broken" in the sense that it cannot run because the system does not have a new enough version of `libseccomp`. 

What negative effect would there be to specifying `libseccomp >= something` where "something" is the version used on the build system?

It's one thing if a package inherently requires a specific version of a package because of some feature, and something different if the requirement is coming from a build system.

I see two potential issues with coding a specific version number in the rpm:
1. If someone were to build from source again on a different build system, a different version of libseccomp will work.  That's probably the case for you, if you were to build the rpm again from source on your 8.1 machine.
2. The build system is a moving target.  Next week the libseccomp might be updated again and cause it to not work on any older system than that version, and making the specific version number listed in the .spec file incorrect for that build.  I don't have any control over what package versions are available on the EPEL build system.

I think this may be an inherent limitation of RPM.  Debian doesn't have this problem.

The rpm built on github is made on centos7, so it probably will work on your 8.1 machine since it is older.  It would be good to know if that is the case.

This is more complicated than I thought when I first opened the issue.  It turns out that most container runtimes (at least the ones I've researched) do not provide a method to delete images from a given registry.  It looks like you can either delete the manifest digest or (less commonly) the tag and then the container data blobs will be deleted on the next garbage collection.  So I think that maybe the best thing that we can do is to provide the manifest digest to the user.  Then they can delete the digest with `curl` or whatever and delete the container with a garbage collect.  Here's the idea.
